flagged.evidence: It defines \(\sigma:U\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-1}\to\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\), then calls the collection of its \(n-1\) tangent vectors and \(B\) an “\(n\times n\) matrix.” These are \(n\) vectors in \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\), so they cannot be columns of an \(n\times n\) matrix or have the asserted determinant. A space-time hypersurface would instead require \(n\) tangent vectors and an \((n+1)\times(n+1)\) determinant.

Step 2.1 says that the columns of \(D\Phi(0,\eta_*)\) are “the \(n-1\) tangent vectors ... together with the transport vector,” and concludes that \(D\Phi\) is invertible. Under the cited Cauchy-surface definition, \(I\times V\) has dimension \(n\) while \(\Phi\) takes values in \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\); its derivative is therefore \((n+1)\times n\), not invertible. Thus the inverse-function-theorem invocation in 3.1 does not follow.

The step says, “Every function of the form \(u(x,t)=F(x-t)\) solves \(u_t+u_x=0\),” without requiring \(F\in C^1\). For \(F(s)=|s|\), \(u(x,t)=|x-t|\) is not differentiable on \(x=t\), hence is not a classical solution in the page's stated classical setting.

The claimed solution \(u(x,t)=u_0(x-bt)\) has no regularity assumption on \(u_0\). With \(n=1\), \(b=0\), and \(u_0(x)=|x|\), the displayed function is not \(C^1\) at \(x=0\), so it is not a classical solution of \(u_t=0\).

Although \(q\) is assumed \(C^1\), no regularity is imposed on \(u_0\). Taking \(n=1\), \(b=0\), \(q=0\), and \(u_0(x)=|x|\) makes the displayed formula \(e^{-t}|x|\), which is not \(C^1\) at \(x=0\) and therefore is not a classical solution.

Step 3.1 derives \(\|Z_h(t)\|_2\le1+M\int_{t_0}^t\|Z_h(s)\|_2\,ds\) for every \(t\in I\). The cited Gronwall theorem requires the forward orientation \(t\ge t_0\) and states a separate reflected form for \(t<t_0\). Indeed, for \(a(x,t)=-x\), \(t_0=0\), and \(I=[-1,1]\), \(Z_h(t)=e^{-t}\) and \(M=1\); at \(t=-1\) the asserted right side is \(1+\int_0^{-1}e^{-s}ds=2-e<0\), while the left side is \(e\). The backward-time argument needs the reflected inequality.
